Laboratory studies of Eisenia fetida maintained at a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] reveal that individuals emerge from their cocoons after an incubation period lasting 25 days [ab = 25 days], a developmental duration that is typical for this species under optimized vermiculture conditions. At the moment of eclosion, the newly emerged juveniles measure approximately 1 centimeter [Lb = approximately 1 centimeter] and possess a wet body mass of 10 milligrams [Wwb = 10 milligrams], reflecting the modest size of the offspring at the onset of their exotrophic phase. The chorionate embryos develop within a protective cocoon matrix that buffers against desiccation and microbial attack. Following yolk absorption completion, these neonates begin active feeding on organic substrates, initiating a rapid growth trajectory that is closely linked to temperature and substrate quality. The duration of this embryonic period compares favorably with reports for other epigeic species, where similar incubation intervals are observed under equivalent thermal regimes.

As the young worms progress through the juvenile stage, they experience a prolonged period of somatic growth before reaching reproductive competence. Under a thermal regime of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the time required from hatching to the attainment of puberty spans roughly 60 days from hatching [tp = roughly 60 days from hatching], a relatively short period that facilitates rapid population turnover in managed systems. At the onset of sexual maturation, individuals typically measure about 5 centimeters [Lp = about 5 centimeters] and have accumulated a wet weight of approximately 275 milligrams [Wwp = approximately 275 milligrams]. This developmental milestone is marked by the formation of the clitellum, a glandular structure essential for cocoon production during copulation. The transition from immature individual to breeding adult coincides with the achievement of a critical body size, beyond which energetic resources are diverted toward gametogenesis onset and reproductive behavior. These growth parameters are consistent with those documented in other vermicomposting species.

When sexually mature adults engage in reproductive activity, each worm produces cocoons at a rate of approximately 2.3 cocoons per worm per week [F_R_i = approximately 2.3 cocoons per worm per week]. Within each cocoon, an average of 2.7 offspring successfully develop and hatch per cocoon [N_R_i = 2.7 offspring successfully develop and hatch per cocoon]. These values, recorded under controlled conditions at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], indicate a substantial reproductive capacity that underpins the species' utility in waste biodegradation systems. The individual offspring per cocoon count aligns well with the findings of Reinecke and Kriel (1981), though Dominguez (2004) has documented slightly broader ranges, typically between 2.5 and 3.8 offspring per cocoon, suggesting a degree of plasticity in reproductive output depending on environmental factors and parental nutrition. The high fecundity rate, coupled with rapid generation times, allows Eisenia fetida to colonize available organic substrates efficiently. The resulting daily reproduction rate, combining these factors, amounts to approximately 0.886 offspring per worm per day [Ri = approximately 0.886 offspring per worm per day].

The maximum adult body size achieved by Eisenia fetida under favorable conditions is approximately 8 centimeters [Li = approximately 8 centimeters], with the largest documented individuals reaching a wet weight of around 1 gram [Wwi = around 1 gram]. This asymptotic size is attained gradually, as growth decelerates markedly following the onset of reproductive allocation. The species exhibits a typical determinate growth pattern, where somatic expansion diminishes in favor of sustained cocoon production over the adult lifespan. Field surveys and laboratory cohorts indicate that maximum recorded longevity for this earthworm reaches roughly 5 years [am = roughly 5 years] under optimal, predator-free captivity at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], although most individuals in natural settings likely senesce earlier due to predation risks and resource fluctuations. This comparatively extended lifespan is unusual among epigeic worms and may reflect the species' adaptation to intermittent resource patches.

Comparative physiological analyses highlight the thermal sensitivity of developmental and reproductive processes in this species, with profound implications for population dynamics in vermiculture operations. For instance, while the 25-day incubation period (25 days) [ab = 25 days] and the roughly 60-day time to puberty from hatching (roughly 60 days from hatching) [tp = roughly 60 days from hatching] are standard at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], deviations from this stable temperature can accelerate or delay these milestones, altering the synchrony between life history transitions and resource availability. Similarly, the maximum reproductive output of approximately 2.3 cocoons per worm per week [F_R_i = approximately 2.3 cocoons per worm per week] and the average of 2.7 offspring per cocoon [N_R_i = average of 2.7 offspring per cocoon] depend critically on thermal stability, with declines in cocoon viability observed outside a narrow thermal optimum. The ultimate wet weight of around 1 gram [Wwi = around 1 gram] and maximum body length of approximately 8 centimeters [Li = approximately 8 centimeters] also represent optimum values achieved under these specific conditions. Future studies should examine how fluctuating thermal environments in outdoor vermiculture operations modulate these life history parameters.
